title: SIMD & Data-Oriented Design
tagline: Do 8–16 lanes of work per instruction — but only if your data is laid out so the CPU can.

concept.analogy: A scalar instruction is one cashier scanning one item at a time. SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) is a cashier with a wide scanner that reads a whole row of items in one swipe. But the wide scanner only works if the items are lined up neatly in a row (contiguous, aligned). Hand it a jumbled pile (pointers scattered across the heap) and it falls back to one-at-a-time. Data-oriented design is the discipline of always presenting the data as a neat row.
paragraphs: Modern CPUs have wide vector registers (SSE 128-bit, AVX2 256-bit, AVX-512 512-bit; NEON/SVE on ARM) that apply one operation to many values at once — e.g., add eight 32-bit floats in a single instruction. Used well, SIMD multiplies arithmetic throughput several-fold for the data-parallel parts of a hot path: computing fair values across a basket, normalizing a vector of prices, scanning for a max, parsing fixed-width fields.

The catch is that SIMD is only as good as your data layout. Vector loads want contiguous, ideally aligned data so a register fills from one cache line; they want Structure-of-Arrays so a single lane operation touches only the field you're processing; and they hate branches inside the kernel (you replace them with masks/blends). Pointer-chasing, AoS, and data-dependent control flow all force the compiler back to scalar code or expensive gather/scatter.

This is why SIMD and data-oriented design (DOD) are taught together. DOD says: organize your program around how data is accessed and transformed in bulk, not around 'objects'. Group hot fields into contiguous arrays (SoA), process them in tight loops, and keep cold/rare data elsewhere. Once the data is in that shape, the compiler's auto-vectorizer can often vectorize the loop for free — and where it can't, you reach for intrinsics or libraries.

For HFT, SIMD shows up in signal computation, risk/PNL aggregation, batch normalization of features, fixed-format message parsing, and checksum/hash routines. The win is throughput, not single-event latency; the meta-lesson is that performance comes from data layout first, then vectorization, then micro-optimization — in that order.
points: SIMD applies one instruction to many lanes (e.g., 8 floats with AVX2).
It needs contiguous, aligned, Structure-of-Arrays data; pointer-chasing and AoS defeat it.
Branches in the kernel become masks/blends; gather/scatter is slow — avoid when possible.
Auto-vectorization often works for free once data is laid out well; intrinsics/libraries for the rest.
Data-oriented design (organize by access pattern, SoA, hot/cold split) is the foundation.

callouts.title: Let the compiler try first
callouts.body: Write clean, contiguous SoA loops with `-O3 -march=native` and check the vectorization report (`-fopt-info-vec` / `-Rpass=loop-vectorize`). Hand-written intrinsics are a last resort — they're unportable and easy to get wrong.

callouts.title: Gather/scatter is a trap
callouts.body: AVX gather loads from non-contiguous addresses, but it's often barely faster than scalar. If you find yourself needing gather, the real fix is usually to change the data layout so loads are contiguous.

concept.keyIdea: SIMD multiplies throughput by operating on many lanes per instruction, but it only delivers when data is contiguous, aligned, and Structure-of-Arrays with branches turned into masks. Fix the data layout (data-oriented design) first; vectorization — often automatic — follows.

deepDive.intro: How to make code vectorizable, when to use intrinsics, and the layout rules that decide whether SIMD helps at all.

steps.title: Make the loop vectorizable
steps.detail: Auto-vectorization needs a countable loop with no loop-carried dependencies, contiguous unit-stride access, no aliasing between input/output (use `__restrict`), and ideally no branches (use arithmetic/masks). Then `-O3 -march=native` lets the compiler emit AVX. Check the report to confirm it actually vectorized and why it didn't if it failed.

steps.title: SoA so each lane is useful
steps.detail: A vector add of prices wants 8 contiguous prices per register. With AoS (price embedded in a fat struct), the prices are 32 bytes apart and you'd need gather. With SoA (`std::vector<float> price`), 8 prices sit in one 32-byte span — one aligned load fills the register. Layout is the enabler.

steps.title: Branches → masks/blends
steps.detail: Inside a SIMD kernel you can't branch per lane. Instead compute a comparison mask (e.g., `_mm256_cmp_ps`) and blend two results (`_mm256_blendv_ps`) or AND with the mask. All lanes do both computations; the mask selects. This is branchless by construction and avoids mispredicts.

steps.title: Alignment, tails, and width
steps.detail: Aligned loads/stores (`_mm256_load_ps` on 32-byte-aligned data) are fastest; handle the leftover 'tail' elements with a scalar epilogue or masked loads. Pick width by target (AVX2 = 8 floats; AVX-512 is wider but can downclock the core — measure, sometimes AVX2 wins overall).

steps.title: Portable options
steps.detail: Beyond raw intrinsics, use `std::experimental::simd`, libraries like xsimd/Highway/Eigen, or `#pragma omp simd` to stay readable and portable across SSE/AVX/NEON. Reserve hand-tuned intrinsics for the few kernels that profiling proves dominate.

notes.title: Throughput, not latency
notes.detail: SIMD speeds up bulk computation; it doesn't shorten the critical path of a single event. Use it for batch signal/PNL/parse work, not to shave one order's tick-to-trade.

notes.title: Watch the clock
notes.detail: Heavy AVX-512 can trigger frequency throttling on some CPUs, so a 'wider' kernel can be net slower for mixed workloads. Always benchmark the whole program, not the kernel in isolation.

notes.title: Reductions need care
notes.detail: Summations vectorize with multiple partial accumulators (to break the dependency chain) then a horizontal add. Be aware floating-point reductions become non-associative — results can differ slightly from the scalar order.

complexity.time: Up to W× fewer instructions (W = lane count)
complexity.timeReason: One vector instruction does W scalar ops. Real speedup is bounded by memory bandwidth, alignment, tails, and how much of the loop actually vectorizes.
complexity.spaceReason: SoA may use the same bytes as AoS but arranged for unit-stride loads; small alignment padding may be added.

pitfalls: Trying to vectorize AoS / pointer-chasing data — you get scalar code or slow gathers.
Per-lane branches instead of masks/blends, reintroducing control flow into the kernel.
Ignoring aliasing (no __restrict) so the compiler refuses to vectorize.
Forgetting the scalar tail or alignment, causing crashes or correctness bugs.
Assuming AVX-512 is always fastest — downclocking can make AVX2 win; measure end-to-end.

benchmark.intro: Elementwise `out = a*k + b` over 64M floats, contiguous data (relative, -O3 -march=native).

cells: 8 lanes + FMA; bandwidth-bound at the top end

benchmark.note: Speedup is capped by memory bandwidth once the kernel is compute-light; layout is the prerequisite.
benchmark.takeaway: Vectorization delivered several-fold throughput only because the data was contiguous SoA. The same SIMD on AoS data would have collapsed to scalar — proving layout comes before vectorization.

interviewQuestions.q: Why are SIMD and Structure-of-Arrays so often discussed together?
a: A SIMD register fills from contiguous memory: to add eight prices in one instruction you need eight prices laid out back-to-back. SoA gives exactly that — each field is its own contiguous array — so a single aligned vector load grabs eight useful values. AoS interleaves fields, so the eight prices are 'struct-stride' apart and you'd need a slow gather or scalar fallback.

So SoA is the enabling data layout for SIMD: it turns a loop over a field into unit-stride, prefetcher-friendly, vectorizable code. That's the heart of data-oriented design — choose the layout that matches how you process the data in bulk.

interviewQuestions.q: When is SIMD the wrong tool, and what does it actually optimize?
a: SIMD optimizes throughput of data-parallel bulk work, not the latency of a single event. It's the wrong tool when the hot path is one event with control-flow-heavy, pointer-chasing logic — there's nothing to vectorize, and forcing it (gathers, per-lane branches) can be slower than clean scalar code.

It's also the wrong first move: if data is AoS or scattered, fix the layout before reaching for intrinsics. And on some CPUs wide AVX-512 downclocks the core, so it can hurt mixed workloads. Use SIMD for batch signal/PNL/feature/parse computations where data is contiguous and you process many elements the same way — and benchmark end-to-end.

interviewQuestions.q: How do you vectorize a sum (reduction), and what subtle correctness issue appears?
a: A naive `for(i) sum += a[i]` has a loop-carried dependency on `sum`, which limits the CPU (each add waits for the previous) and a single accumulator can't fill a vector register usefully. To vectorize, use multiple partial accumulators — e.g., maintain a vector of 8 partial sums, add 8 lanes per iteration (independent adds, breaking the dependency chain and using the full SIMD width), and at the end do a horizontal add to combine the lanes into the final scalar. Compilers do this automatically with `-O3 -ffast-math` (or `#pragma omp simd reduction`), or you write it with intrinsics.

The subtle correctness issue is that floating-point addition is *not associative*: summing in a different order (lane-wise then horizontal, vs strictly left-to-right) can give a slightly different result due to rounding. So the vectorized sum is not bit-identical to the scalar one — which is why compilers require `-ffast-math`/`-fassociative-math` (or an explicit reduction clause) to reorder FP reductions, since it technically changes results. For most analytics this is fine (and often *more* accurate), but if you need reproducibility or are doing money math, be deliberate: use integer/fixed-point where exactness matters, or a defined summation order, and document that the vectorized result may differ in the last bits.

problems.title: Make a loop vectorize, then beat it with intrinsics
problems.statement: You have two AoS arrays of `struct Q{float bid; float ask; float last; int id;}`. A hot routine computes `mid[i] = 0.5f*(bid+ask)` for a million entries and it won't vectorize. Diagnose why, refactor so the compiler auto-vectorizes it, and then write an AVX2 intrinsic version. State how you'd verify the speedup and correctness.
problems.hint: The fields you need (bid, ask) aren't contiguous in AoS; move to SoA, add __restrict, then check the vectorizer report.

approach: Why it won't vectorize: in AoS, bid/ask are 16 bytes apart (struct stride), so the loop has strided access — the compiler must gather, which it usually declines, leaving scalar code. Aliasing uncertainty between input and output pointers can also block it.

Refactor to SoA: keep `std::vector<float> bid, ask, mid;`. Now `for(i) mid[i]=0.5f*(bid[i]+ask[i]);` is unit-stride. Mark pointers `__restrict` (or pass distinct vectors) so the compiler knows they don't alias, build with `-O3 -march=native`, and confirm with `-Rpass=loop-vectorize` / `-fopt-info-vec` that it emitted AVX.

Intrinsic version: load 8 bids and 8 asks (`_mm256_loadu_ps`), add, multiply by a broadcast 0.5 (`_mm256_mul_ps`), store; scalar tail for the remainder. Verify: compare outputs against the scalar version within a tiny float tolerance for correctness, and microbenchmark all three (AoS scalar, SoA auto-vec, SoA intrinsic) over the same data, plus `perf stat` to confirm higher IPC and that you're now bandwidth-bound.

problems.title: Redesign a struct for SIMD and measure
problems.statement: A risk engine stores positions as `struct Pos { double qty; double price; char sym[8]; uint32_t acct; };` in a vector, and a hot routine computes total notional = Σ qty*price over millions of positions, but it won't vectorize well. Redesign the layout, write a vectorizable (or intrinsic) notional sum, and describe how you'd verify both the speedup and that the result is acceptable.
problems.hint: AoS interleaves qty/price with sym/acct, so vector loads can't fill cleanly; move to SoA (separate qty[] and price[]) and use a multi-accumulator/FMA reduction.

approach: Why it won't vectorize: in AoS, each Pos is ~28–32 bytes, so qty and price for consecutive positions are strided ~32 bytes apart and interleaved with sym/acct. A SIMD load can't grab 8 contiguous qtys; you'd need slow gathers, and the loop also has a reduction dependency on the running sum.

Redesign to SoA: store `std::vector<double> qty, price;` (and sym/acct separately). Now qty[i] and price[i] are each dense and contiguous, so the loop `Σ qty[i]*price[i]` is unit-stride and vectorizable: load 8 qtys and 8 prices, multiply, and accumulate with FMA into several partial-sum vectors (multiple accumulators to break the dependency chain), then horizontal-add at the end. The compiler will auto-vectorize the clean SoA loop with `-O3 -march=native -ffast-math`, or write it with AVX2 intrinsics.

Verify: (1) speedup — microbenchmark AoS-scalar vs SoA-auto-vec vs SoA-intrinsic over the same data; check `perf stat` shows higher IPC and that you've become memory-bandwidth-bound (the sign you've maxed the kernel). Confirm the vectorizer fired with `-Rpass=loop-vectorize`. (2) Correctness/acceptability — because the FP reduction order changed (lane-wise + horizontal vs left-to-right), the result may differ in the last bits; verify it's within an acceptable tolerance of the scalar result, and if exact reproducibility is required (e.g., official risk numbers), use a fixed summation order or higher-precision/Kahan summation. Expect a several-fold throughput gain, gated by the layout change, not the SIMD itself.
